- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤ -0.33) in recent days, model often underestimates downside; adjust downward bias or add early correction factor.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >85.0), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply lagged mean reversion or cap forecast at +5–10% above peak.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa), model lags in adjusting; introduce sentiment-weighted smoothing or delay correction by 1–2 periods.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80), model often fails to recognize it; reduce forecast slope and add downward bias adjustment.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to be overly optimistic in early periods (e.g., first 5–7 days); apply downward bias of 1–2% per day if sentiment is neutral or bearish.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative sentiment (e.g., 3+ consecutive negative values), model often fails to anticipate sharp drops; add early warning buffer or reduce forecast by 3–5% for next period.
